title: Stage 3 sacral pressure ulcer with copious exudate in end-stage COPD palliative unit patient
scenario_text: Mrs. Komala Kunhiraman, 81F, end-stage GOLD IV COPD with cor pulmonale, PPS 20, admitted to a 30-bed palliative unit in Kozhikode, Kerala (NGO-run, well-resourced for India) for 2 weeks now. Comorbidities: Type 2 diabetes on insulin, AF on aspirin (warfarin stopped 3 months ago because of falls), prior MI, albumin 2.2, severe cachexia BMI 14.5. She has a Stage 3 sacral pressure ulcer (full-thickness skin loss, exposing subcutaneous fat, no muscle/bone exposed, ~6 cm x 5 cm x 2 cm depth, sloughy yellow base ~40%, granulating ~50%, exudate moderate-heavy serous, no obvious infection, no fever, mild surrounding erythema). She is on triple inhaler, morphine 5 mg PO Q4H (for dyspnea + pain), LTOT 2 L/min, lorazepam 0.5 mg SL PRN, insulin sliding scale. Family son and daughter present. ASHA-equivalent palliative attendant has done wound care training and asks the senior palliative physician (currently on phone): she wants to know which dressing system, antibiotic prophylaxis, debridement, pain control during dressing, and family discussion points.

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: End-stage GOLD IV COPD with cor pulmonale, Stage 3 sacral pressure ulcer, severe cachexia
current_medications: Morphine IR 5 mg PO Q4H + 5 mg Q1-2H PRN
Insulin NPH 6 units HS + sliding scale regular

presenting_complaint: Stage 3 sacral pressure ulcer with moderate-heavy exudate and slough — needs structured wound management plan in end-of-life context.
asker_query: Doctor, amma has a deep bed sore on her back — about 6 cm across, 2 cm deep, yellow slough in middle and pink edges, heavy fluid soaks the dressing. No smell, no fever. She is bedbound on morphine 5 mg every 4 hours. How should we dress it? Antibiotic? Will it heal or are we just keeping her comfortable?
ideal_response_components: Frame honestly and compassionately: at PPS 20, BMI 14.5, albumin 2.2, end-stage COPD — Stage 3 ulcer is unlikely to fully heal; goals are now COMFORT, EXUDATE CONTROL, PREVENTION OF INFECTION, AND DIGNITY rather than complete healing

Wound bed preparation: gentle autolytic debridement of slough using hydrogel (e.g. Intrasite, Solugel) under absorbent dressing; AVOID sharp surgical debridement (no benefit at end of life, causes pain/bleeding); avoid aggressive scrubbing

Dressing system for heavy exudate: primary contact layer (non-adherent paraffin gauze or hydrogel for slough); secondary super-absorbent foam dressing (e.g. Mepilex/Allevyn) or alginate (e.g. Kaltostat) — alginate especially good for heavy exudate; change every 2-3 days or when strikethrough; for malodour (if develops): topical metronidazole gel 0.75% applied to wound or crushed metronidazole tablet sprinkled — strong evidence

Pain on dressing: 30 min before dressing — give breakthrough morphine 5 mg PO; consider topical 2% lidocaine gel on wound surface for direct pain (off-label but evidence supports in palliative wound care); use atraumatic technique

Antibiotic: NO routine systemic antibiotic for non-infected Stage 3 ulcer — selects resistance; treat ONLY if signs of cellulitis (spreading erythema, fever, increased pain, purulent foul discharge); topical silver dressing (e.g. Acticoat) can be used if heavy bioburden suspected (consult; not routine)
Continue pressure offloading despite the ulcer being present: 2-hourly turns, alternating mattress, 30° lateral tilt, float heels — to prevent additional ulcers and reduce progression

Nutrition: cannot expect healing without nutrition substrate, but at PPS 20 forcing intake is inappropriate; offer comfort feeding — soft Malayali foods she likes (kanji, banana, jackfruit, milk, dal); supplemental shake (if accepted); do NOT insert NG/PEG just for ulcer healing — does not improve outcomes
Diabetes: relax insulin targets — fasting 150-220 mg/dL acceptable; daily insulin review to avoid hypoglycaemia given declining intake
Pain control review: she is on morphine 5 mg Q4H for baseline; if more pain on movement/dressing, may need scheduled increase to 7.5 mg Q4H + breakthrough; review with palliative physician

Family conversation: explicit and tender — 'amma's wound is part of her body now slowing down; we will keep it clean, keep her comfortable, control the smell and fluid, prevent infection; healing fully is unlikely at this stage; this does not mean we have failed; comfort is success'
Documentation: photograph wound weekly (with daughter's consent), measure size, depth, slough %, exudate level, surrounding skin — for trend monitoring
Spiritual/family presence: encourage daughter to be at the bedside, music, prayers, gentle touch — comfort dimensions beyond the wound
expected_guideline_citations: EWMA Position Document on Wound Bed Preparation
EPUAP Guidance on Palliative Wound Care
Pallium India Module — Wound care in advanced palliative care
IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care 2nd ed. — End-of-life wound care
WHO Palliative Care for Non-Cancer Conditions
safety_traps: Sharp surgical debridement at end of life — causes pain and bleeding without benefit
Empirical systemic antibiotic for non-infected ulcer — selects resistance, GI side effects
Inserting NG/PEG for 'nutrition to heal ulcer' — not evidence-supported in this setting, harms quality of life
Using Dettol / hydrogen peroxide / undiluted povidone-iodine on wound bed — cytotoxic
Forcing tight diabetes control in cachectic end-of-life patient — hypoglycaemia harm
Not pre-medicating for dressing change — preventable suffering
Setting unrealistic healing goal with family — leads to guilt and frustration
Failing to offer topical metronidazole if odour develops — distressing for patient and family
Stopping aspirin without weighing benefit (AF cardio-protection) vs minimal bleeding risk from ulcer — discuss case by case
indian_context_notes: Kerala has well-developed palliative network (NNPC) and good supply chain for hydrogel, alginate, foam dressings — but rural NGO supply variable, may need to use cheaper paraffin gauze + super-absorbent pads
Malayalam-language family communication essential; Kerala has strong tradition of family-led palliative care
Topical metronidazole gel (Metrogyl 1%) widely available and cheap in Kerala (~₹50/tube); crushed metronidazole tablet alternative ₹2/tab
Sandalwood / coconut oil massage tradition — must counsel NOT to apply oils to ulcer bed (only intact surrounding skin if soothing)
Daughter as 50F primary family caregiver — common Kerala pattern; explicit recognition of her work prevents burnout
Pallium India / Institute of Palliative Medicine, Kozhikode is THE major training centre — protocols here are reference quality
